items.title: Show HN: MeowDisplay Is iPhone Mirroring, but in Reverse
items.summary: Hey HN and Cats, thank you for checking this out! Github: https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay MeowDisplay is my take on the control your Mac from your phone scene. Available on iPhones, iPads and Macs, with Android rn in closed testing. The website has interactive illustrative demos if you'd like to see the app demonstrated. I think MeowDisplay does a few things differently, some of which I prefer and you might too. Such as Window view: allowing multiple tabs in split-screen type panes. Traditional Mirror/Extend views exist as alternatives. Floating windows: coming in the 2.1 release. Touch input approaches: Direct Touch(Classic or Natural), experimental Smart Touch, and Trackpad mode alongside Apple Pencil support. Doesn't sacrifice display space for a trackpad, use all of the phone's screen with your preferred mode. Stage Peek: shows a scrollable and searchable list of your Mac's windows on your phone along with an app drawer when you hold and pull on the left edge of your screen. It's free and open source so you can try it and see if it's for you without having to commit to it or anything. EDIT: I've used MeowDisplay during development whilst I was travelling between cities, left my acbook at home clamshell, powered, external display attached, and used it for small tasks remotely, it was pretty reliable even on a 5G network on a moving bus. Meow, Jai

Show HN: DBDelve – Open-Source DB Client Made with Rust and GPUI
items.summary: Hi HN, I’m Shayan and a few months ago I started building a DB Client DBDelve with a focus on performance and just making something that feels good to use (in the spirit of Zed, Ghostty, and other tools that just feel pleasant to use). For my workflow I’ve always looked for performance, especially since some time ago I had a really outdated machine and any kind of bloat was really noticeable, I remember using DBeaver and it just crashing on me multiple times, I also had to use postGIS which just made it worse. I migrated all my essential dev tools to use the ones with performance in mind (Zed, Ghostty etc) but the only thing that was missing was DB Client. The main choices everyone has are DBeaver which is a memory hog and an overkill for most of the tasks imo. The other options like Datagrid, Beekeeper, TablePlus are either electron based so bloated and memory hogs or paid and closed-source. DBDelve 0.3.6 against DBeaver 25.3.1 on the same Postgres table, median of 5 runs each (2026-10-11, M1 Pro, 32 GB). Times are from the action to the rows rendered. DBDelve DBeaver Launch 1.1 s 5.2 s Idle memory 133 MB 606 MB 1,000-row query 0.21 s 1.96 s 1M rows, time 56 s 208 s 1M rows, memory [1] 4.9 GB 17 GB [1] The whole 1M-row, 100-column table pulled into memory on purpose, with the row limit off. Not a normal use case; DBeaver's heap limit had to be raised manually for the benchmark. Scrolling perf with 1 million rows loaded with 100 columns each: https://youtu.be/V2MOhJYFqIE It has most of the features most devs would need for 90% of their workflow plus some more I thought would be a nice touch: Readonly, read-write and Full Access modes Glass themes (If you’re into them, I am) Keyboard focused with every keybinding customizable Organization of connections into projects Me and some other folks have been daily driving it for more than a month now and most good feedback comes on it having a really simple UI to navigate, very stable for its age and the performance of course. I’m also sharing here because those people tell me this has potential to grow so I’m trying my hand at distributing it. Just want to give a huge shoutout here to the Zed team for GPUI, it's a breeze to work with if you just get through them not updating the crate officially on crates.io but the community has found the solutions for it, you just have to dig deep for it. It performs extremely well and just the HTML-like structure of it, makes it easy to understand for someone from a web dev background and agents are very good at writing it too. GPUI component also solves a lot of problems with having a good component library we can use. I think for anyone starting a GPUI project now, GPUI-kit makes a lot of sense, it just bundles GPUI, GPUI-component together and has some optimizations adding retained mode which is experimental but could provide a lot of benefit, so think all things considered it should be the default way. The major optimization I did was just lowering the memory overhead by using packed rows which reduced the memory usage by 40% on large datasets (8.1GB to 4.9GB on a 4GB table loaded in app), everything else came bundled in with Rust and GPUI mostly or they just made it very easy. Limitations: It's not signed and notarized, identity verification from apple's side has been a nightmare but it should be signed soon. Don’t expect feature parity with more mature clients for now, the general direction of this right now is the zed way of adding features in but after making sure the core workflows are done with a high quality. Do give it a try, you can import your connections from dbeaver and tableplus. https://github.com/ShayanAbbas1/dbdelve

Show HN: TimeScroll – an open-source, local replacement for Rewind on Mac
items.summary: Hi HN, I've been building TimeScroll since September 2025. It's a Mac app that records your screen in the background, so you can scroll back through your day or search for anything you've seen. It is local and open-source. The key features are introduced on the site, so I'll try to reduce the repetition in this post. My motivation for building was (1) Rewind shutting down and the lack of alternatives that are as polished and direct; (2) Most apps like this (including Rewind really) are super CPU and storage intensive, to the point of having a noticeable impact on your battery life. I identified a few issues with the 'standard' way of capturing and made it a point to fix them in this app. 1. The part I spent the most time on is how the text gets captured. Basically all the apps run OCR on every screenshot, which means the heavy OCR step will always take a certain amount of CPU. I noticed that the text is already inside the apps, so I took the completely different approach of reading it through the macOS Accessibility API instead (which I call Direct mode). It has big advantages - gets the exact text with no misread characters, along with the position of each line, and it's much cheaper than OCR. The problem was that Chrome and Electron apps don't work very well with it, as they wouldn't create an accessibility tree unless requested, so I needed to set AXManualAccessibility attribute. Also, the text can be buried under many layers of the tree, so I have to write logic to traverse the tree within a time limit and capture as much useful text as possible. I haven't seen any screen capture app do these, so I had to figure most of it out on my own. There are also a lot of implementation details - like first computing which windows are on each display and which parts of them are visible on screen. Ultimately, my measurements were around 9ms of CPU time to read a frame initially, but on subsequent reads, it can go as low as 0.4 ms. The newest feature is summaries. You can select any range on the timeline and get your time in each app plus a written summary from a local model through Ollama. The main implementation trick used in the summary is (1) dividing the usage into 'sessions' using heuristics and (2) using the existing embeddings (from AI search) to choose a few representative screens to pass to the model. 2. Storage optimizations. I chose HEVC video to store the snapshots with one "segment" file per minute. The encoding process was something I needed to tune over time. Currently, I am using a constant quality setting with one keyframe per segment. On text-heavy frames, the approach I used managed to reduce it from 84 KB per frame to 20 KB, at slightly better quality. There is also a lot of duplicate text that would multiply the storage use if stored for each snapshot, so deduplication and compression were huge things to figure out. Needless to say, all of this took many tries to get right, especially working with extracting/storing frames to the video files efficiently. The end result is that TimeScroll uses ~2GB/month with normal daily usage and averages 1.1% CPU and 150-250MB memory on an M4 over a few days of normal use, whereas an older post about Rewind I found measured it to be "200MB/hour" and 20% CPU, which is ... a lot in comparison. There are a lot of other things and approaches I tried that I can't fit here, but anyways, I'd really like feedback, especially on Direct mode and on the newer features - hope you enjoy the app!
